value: significant daily changes in absolute sensitivity to stimuli of different colors; no daily changes in spectral sensitivity
method: electrophysiological: ERG from the right compound eye, sensitivity at 12 wavelengths (366-633 nm) every 6 h to a criterion amplitude (0.5 mV or near threshold), light intensity set with neutral density filters
conditions: Adults of both sexes caught in summer in bushes near Graz and kept in the laboratory for a few days under natural ambient light and temperature, with no fixed light-dark regime stated; recordings at 20-23 C in a shielded chamber after more than 120 min of dark adaptation; the start of the 24 h experiment was varied between noon, evening, midnight and morning; N = 6 in the tables; the paper reports clock time and does not state that recording time was matched to each animal's circadian phase; Results give the direction of the change (about 1 log unit more sensitive at midnight than at noon in the blue-green to green region) and a broad green maximum (546 nm) that stayed the same; the insects were kept in absolute darkness throughout the 24 h experiment; a control ERG 6 h after the end, at the same time of day as the first, had to agree within 10%, which 60% of the insects did, and only those were analysed

source.title: Daily visual sensitivity pattern in the green lacewing Chrysoperla carnea (Neuroptera: Chrysopidae)

quote: 24-hour experiments on dark-adapted compound eyes of the green lacewing, Chrysoperla carnea (Stephens) show significant daily changes in absolute sensitivity to stimuli of different colors, but no daily changes in the spectral sensitivity.
note: Nocturnal-to-diurnal swing in eye sensitivity of a lacewing: the next abstract sentence reads 'The absolute sensitivity is highest for all wavelengths at mid night, and lowest at noon.' The article page prints CC BY 4.0; no DOI is shown on the page or the PDF, and a Crossref title search finds none. The paper's green maximum (546 nm) is probably the source of the lambda_max_nm 546 row on main from van der Kooi et al. 2021 (methods unit), which compiles it; that row is a different trait. The same paper reports a pseudopupil acceptance angle widest at midnight (not filed here).

value: mean 36 gaze shifts per minute, mean gaze duration 1.7 s
method: behavioural: passive observation, with the number of times the animal shifted its visual field by moving its eyes or head counted in 60 s bins
conditions: Free-living lizards watched in the open field at the Indio Mountains Research Station on 10-12 August, generally at air temperature 30-35 C, at various hours; observation passive at a non-obtrusive distance; this species was the stated exception to the usual 10-20 min episodes because it was very skittish and hard to follow, the exact number of animals and sessions is not given, but each observation was of a different individual and the Results place it among lizards with 3 or more sessions; the count is a behavioural proxy for gaze redirection and not a measure of retinal scanning; the other lizard species were watched in museum terraria, so the settings differ; the quoted sentence is in the Discussion (4.1 Lizards)

source.title: What is it like to be a lizard? Directed attention and the flow of sensory experience in lizards and birds

quote: The striped whiptail shifted its gaze a mean of 36 times per minute (a mean gaze duration of just 1.7 s).
note: Highest gaze-shift rate of any lizard in the paper, and a statistical outlier among them (ROUT, probability above 98%; differs from each other clade, p < 0.0001); the paper states CC BY and Crossref lists CC BY 4.0. The text calls the animal the striped whiptail; the Methods list it as the little striped whiptail, Aspidoscelis inornata (Reptile Database spelling: Aspidoscelis inornatus Baird, 1859). Each observation of this species was on a different individual, and the Results count it among lizards with 3 or more sessions.

value: bilaterally blinded muskellunge do not stalk their prey and lunge only at prey at close range
method: behavioural: videotaped strikes on live fathead minnows in a test arena after bilateral optic nerve transection
conditions: Abstract only; subadult muskellunge, five test groups (intact controls, lateral line suppressed, bilaterally blinded, unilaterally blinded, unilateral lateral line denervated); prey were fathead minnows (Pimephales promelas); blinding was by optic nerve transection, so the surgery itself is a possible influence; group sizes, tank and light conditions, trial order and statistics are not in the abstract and the full text was not available to this unit; the same abstract says vision is used in the initial acquisition of prey

source.authors: New JG, Fewkes LA, Khan AN
source.title: Strike feeding behavior in the muskellunge, Esox masquinongy: contributions of the lateral line and visual sensory systems

quote: Bilaterally blinded muskellunge do not stalk their prey, but will lunge only at prey that are at close range.
note: First Esox row on main. Journal licence is the Company of Biologists user licence, not open; abstract read as deposited by the publisher in Crossref (identical on ScienceOpen).

value: lateral-line-suppressed muskellunge strongly alter their approaches to more distant prey
method: behavioural: videotaped approach and strike on fathead minnows after lateral line afference was suppressed by 12-24 h immersion in 0.1 mmol/l CoCl2
conditions: Abstract only; subadult muskellunge compared with intact control animals; CoCl2 immersion suppresses lateral line input but can act on other tissues, and no sham-immersion group is described in the abstract; group sizes, tank and light conditions, trial order and statistics are not in the abstract and the full text was not available to this unit; the abstract adds that the lateral line system may play a critical role in the final capture of the prey

source.authors: New JG, Fewkes LA, Khan AN
source.title: Strike feeding behavior in the muskellunge, Esox masquinongy: contributions of the lateral line and visual sensory systems

quote: In addition, lateral-line-suppressed muskellunge strongly alter their approaches to more distant prey.
note: Behavioural role of the lateral line in a pike (genus Esox); abstract read as deposited by the publisher in Crossref (identical on ScienceOpen). The same abstract says both vision and the lateral line determine the initiation of the strike.

value: surviving larvae from the harsh heat stress regime had higher vibration responsiveness
method: behavioural: distance from the trap at which a larva reacted to sand delivered through a funnel (1 mL from 5 cm), tested at 15, 12, 9, 6, 3 and 0 cm, scored blind to rearing regime
conditions: Laboratory test of second-instar larvae collected in June 2020 and housed singly in sand-filled cups; 100 larvae in 50 mass-matched pairs, one of each pair reared at a constant 30 C (mild) and one at 36 C (harsh) in darkness until the molt to third instar, then held 72 h at 20 C and tested; the harsh regime raised mortality, so the comparison is among survivors (of the larvae that survived to testing, 2 of 24 from the harsh and 5 of 34 from the mild regime did not respond, Fisher p = 0.688), and the authors offer two explanations, removal of poorly perceiving larvae or compensatory hunting by survivors; reaction was more frequent in harsh-regime larvae (z = 3.622, P < 0.001); vibration amplitude was not measured, only the sand volume and drop height; the responsiveness model used responding larvae only; the authors note that larger, more food-limited larvae did not show a stronger regime effect, which weakens the compensation explanation

source.title: Heat stress during development makes antlion larvae more responsive to vibrational cues

quote: Furthermore, among the individuals who remained alive, those originating from the harsh heat stress regime were characterized by higher vibration responsiveness.
note: Developmental heat changes vibration responsiveness in an antlion; the copy read prints Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial. All larvae responded more to cues delivered from nearer distances.
